why.correct: With the tax, the quantity traded falls below the efficient quantity, where MSB (demand) meets MSC (supply). The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and supply from the quantity after the tax out to the efficient quantity (region dwl).

The subsidy pushes the quantity past the efficient quantity. For those extra units the cost to society (on S, the MSC) is above their benefit (on D, the MSB). The deadweight loss is the triangle between S and D from the efficient quantity out to the new, larger quantity (region dwl).

At the ceiling, sellers supply less than the efficient quantity, so the quantity traded falls. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and supply from that smaller quantity out to the efficient quantity (region dwl).

The monopoly produces where MR = MC, less than the allocatively efficient quantity where demand (MSB) meets MC (MSC). The deadweight loss is the area between demand and MC from the monopoly quantity to that efficient quantity (region dwl), not out to ATC.
With no benefits or costs falling on others, demand is MSB and supply is MSC, so the efficient point is where they cross: the market equilibrium.
The units beyond the efficient quantity cost more to make (MSC) than they are worth to buyers (MSB); the gap summed over those units is area g.
options: That is the cost of the subsidy to the government, most of which goes to buyers and sellers.
Area c is a gain to buyers from the lower price.
Right: the triangle between supply and demand beyond the original equilibrium, out to the new quantity.
Area a is consumer surplus before the subsidy.

why.correct: A unit should be made only if its MSB is at least its MSC. The subsidy leads to units where MSC > MSB, which is why there is deadweight loss.
options: Right: past the efficient quantity, supply lies above demand.
That holds for units below the efficient quantity, not for the last one produced with the subsidy.
They are equal only at the efficient quantity, which is smaller.
The subsidy shifts who pays; the cost to society of making the ride is unchanged.

why.correct: Here the original equilibrium was efficient. Any policy that moves the quantity away from it, in either direction, creates deadweight loss.
options: The subsidy raises the quantity.
Supply shifted right with the subsidy, so the quantity changed.
Who pays does not stop the quantity from rising.
Right: supply shifts right and the new crossing is beyond the original equilibrium.

why.correct: Open each hour whose MSB is at least its MSC. The third hour gives $12 of benefit for $8 of cost; the fourth gives $9 for $10. So 3 hours.
Hours 4 and 5 should not run. Hour 4 loses $10 - $9 = $1 and hour 5 loses $12 - $6 = $6, so $7 in all.
The third hour should run but does not. It would have added $12 - $8 = $4 of surplus, so $4 is lost.
A competitive market with no third-party effects reaches MSB = MSC on its own.
options: A monopoly sets price above MC and produces too little.
Right: with competition and no effects on others, D = MSB and S = MSC, so the equilibrium is efficient.
A binding price ceiling cuts the quantity supplied below the efficient quantity.
A subsidy pushes the quantity past the efficient quantity.

why.correct: Subsidies in an otherwise efficient market lead to overproduction; monopoly and binding ceilings lead to underproduction.
options: Its equilibrium is efficient.
The monopoly restricts output, so it makes too little.
At the low fare, fewer rides are supplied: too little.
Right: the subsidy pushes bread output past the efficient quantity.

why.correct: Allocative efficiency needs P = MC. A monopoly stops where MR = MC, below the efficient quantity.
options: Profit is a transfer from buyers; the loss comes from units not produced.
Right: at the monopoly quantity MSB (price) > MSC (MC).
A monopoly charges more than MC.
It produces less than the efficient quantity.

why.correct: Below the efficient quantity, each added unit is worth more than it costs; above it, less. Total surplus is largest at MSB = MSC.
options: Total benefit keeps rising while MSB is positive; the efficient point weighs cost too.
A low price says nothing about whether each unit is worth its cost.
Profit is the firm's goal, not society's; a monopoly's profit-maximizing quantity is too small.
Right: MSB = MSC.

why.correct: A market fails when it leaves deadweight loss: too much or too little is made compared with MSB = MSC.
options: Right: the market produces a quantity other than the one where MSB = MSC.
Losses and exit are a normal part of competitive markets.
Fast price changes can be efficient responses to shifts.
Government policy can cause inefficiency, but that is not the definition.

why.correct: The deadweight loss is a triangle: ½ × 40 × $10 = $200.
Underproduction leaves units with MSB > MSC unmade; that lost net benefit is the deadweight loss.
options: That describes units beyond the efficient quantity.
Equality holds only at the efficient quantity.
Right: society would gain by making it.
Neither is zero just because the unit is not made.

why.correct: Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus, and it is largest at the efficient quantity. Any other quantity leaves deadweight loss.
options: Units past MSB = MSC cost more than they are worth.
A price ceiling can raise consumer surplus while lowering total surplus.
A monopoly can raise producer surplus while creating deadweight loss.
Right: that is the quantity where MSB = MSC.

why.correct: A binding floor moves the quantity traded away from MSB = MSC, so total surplus falls.
options: Higher prices for sellers are a transfer; the lost units are a loss.
Right: at the floor, quantity demanded falls below the efficient quantity.
The quantity traded changes even though the curves do not.
At a price above equilibrium, buyers buy less, not more.

why.correct: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis. Demand is D = MPB = MSB (no benefit falls on others). Supply is S = MPC, the firms' own cost. MSC lies above S by the external cost per unit.
Buyers and sellers look only at private benefit and private cost, so the market settles where MPB, the demand curve, meets MPC, the supply curve.
Efficiency counts every cost: the efficient point is where MSB, here the demand curve, meets MSC, at a smaller quantity and a higher price than the market's.

Units between the efficient quantity and the market quantity cost society more (MSC) than they are worth (MSB). The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and D from the efficient quantity to the market quantity, pointing toward the efficient quantity (region dwl).
The tax raises each firm's marginal cost by the external cost, so supply shifts up (left) onto MSC. The new equilibrium is the efficient one: a higher price and a smaller quantity.
MSB lies above demand (MPB) by the external benefit. The efficient point is where MSB meets MSC, here the supply curve: a larger quantity than the market makes.

A subsidy to buyers raises what each buyer gains from a shot, so demand shifts right onto MSB. The new equilibrium is the efficient quantity, larger than before, at a higher price received by sellers.

MSC lies below S (MPC) by the external benefit, so the market makes less than the efficient quantity, where D meets MSC. The deadweight loss is the triangle between D and MSC from the market quantity to the efficient quantity (region dwl).
Deadweight loss counts only the units that should not be made, and only the amount by which their MSC exceeds their MSB.
options: Together these are the total external cost of every unit the market makes.
Area c lies between D and S beyond the efficient quantity; it is part of what buyers and sellers gain on those units.
Right: the triangle between MSC and D from the efficient quantity to the market quantity.
Area b is the external cost of units that are worth making.

why.correct: The external cost per unit is the vertical gap between MSC and MPC. Summed over every unit made, it is the whole band out to the market quantity.
options: Right: the band between MSC and S from zero to the market quantity.
Area a is the deadweight loss only.
That leaves out area a, which is also between MSC and S.
That is the external cost of the efficient quantity only.

why.correct: With a negative externality, MSC > MPC, so the market overproduces and charges too low a price.
options: Demand is unchanged; the extra cost falls on people outside the market.
Competition reaches MSB = MSC only when sellers bear every cost.
The overproduction comes from the cost side, not from buyers.
Right: they produce where MPB = MPC, beyond where MSB = MSC.

why.correct: The market uses private curves (MPB = MPC); efficiency uses social curves (MSB = MSC).
options: The market ignores the fumes, so it makes more, not less.
Right: MPB = MPC at 50 ($10), and MSB = MSC at 40 ($12).
At 50 tons MSC ($14) is above MSB ($10).
At 60 tons MPC ($12) is above MPB ($8), so the market stops sooner.

why.correct: Set the tax equal to the external cost per unit at the efficient quantity: MSC - MPC at 40 tons = $12 - $8 = $4 per ton. Firms then face the full social cost.
Between 40 and 50 tons, MSC is above MSB. At 50 tons the gap is $14 - $10 = $4, and at 40 tons it is zero. DWL = ½ × (50 - 40) × $4 = $20.
Tax revenue = tax × quantity after the tax = $4 × 40 = $160.
Sort by two questions: does it help or harm others, and does it come from making the good or from using it?
options: That is a cost from production: a negative production externality.
Right: using (consuming) the shot benefits other people.
That benefit comes from a firm's production: a positive production externality.
That is a cost from consumption: a negative consumption externality.

why.correct: A negative consumption externality puts MSB below the demand curve (MPB), so the market quantity exceeds the efficient quantity.
options: That would be a benefit to others, not a cost.
The cost comes from using the fireworks, not making them, so it is shown on the benefit side.
The neighbors bear a cost that buyers ignore.

why.correct: The external benefit comes from consumption, so pay buyers per unit: the subsidy shifts demand to MSB.
options: Right: it raises buyers' benefit to match MSB, so more people get the shot.
A tax would lower the quantity, but the market already makes too few.
A payment that does not depend on the number given does not change the quantity.

A cost the firm pays itself is a private cost.

options: Only a per-unit tax changes the cost of the last unit and so the quantity.
A fixed fee is paid whatever the output; it gives no reason to make more.
With MC unchanged, output does not change.

why.correct: A corrective (Pigouvian) subsidy equals the external benefit per unit at the efficient quantity: MSB - MPB = $13 - $10 = $3.
Negative production externality: MSC > MPC, market Q > efficient Q, market P < efficient P.
options: That is the pattern of a positive production externality.
Right: firms do not pay the external cost, so supply is too far right.
With a negative production externality MSC lies above MPC.

why.correct: A per-unit tax equal to the external cost, on either side of the market, makes buyers and sellers face the full social cost of the last unit.
options: Right: it shifts supply up to MSC.
It leaves marginal cost, price and quantity unchanged.

A floor below the market price does not bind, so price and quantity do not change.

why.correct: A public good is both nonrival and nonexcludable.

The problem is collecting payment, not the show's value.

Light on a street is nonrival: all three use it at once.
The problem is collecting payment for a nonexcludable good.

why.correct: This is the tragedy of the commons: open access to a rival resource leads to overuse.

A fish caught is gone: fish are rival.

options: That is rivalry.

Public goods are nonrival.

options: Right: nonrival and nonexcludable.
The fare box excludes nonpayers: at most a club good while the bus has room.
Rival: one rider's seat is not available to another.
Excludable: there is a ticket gate.
Rival and nonexcludable: a common resource.

options: Right: nonrival (while uncrowded) and excludable.
The gate makes it excludable.
A common resource is rival and nonexcludable.

Rivalry depends on use; a crowded road is rival.

With a gate it stays excludable.

why.correct: The allocatively efficient price is where demand meets MC. With the ceiling there, the ceiling becomes the firm's marginal revenue out to demand, so the firm produces where MC equals the ceiling: more output at a lower price than without regulation.

Allocative efficiency needs P = MC, so the board sets the price where the demand curve crosses MC (the socially optimal price). Because ATC is above MC there, the company would make a loss without a subsidy.
Up to demand, each unit sells at the ceiling, so MR equals the ceiling and the firm produces where MC meets it: the point where demand crosses MC, more output at a lower price than unregulated.
A normal profit (zero economic profit) means price equals ATC, so the regulated price is at the height where demand crosses ATC: the fair-return price.
Unregulated, it produces where MR = MC and reads the price from demand. Profit is the rectangle between that price and ATC at that quantity, from zero out to the quantity (region profit).
MR = MC = $2 at 4 thousand units. The price from demand is $6 and ATC is $5, so profit = (P - ATC) × Q = ($6 - $5) × 4 = 4 thousand dollars.
The fair-return price is where the demand curve meets ATC, so the firm earns zero economic profit.
options: That is the socially optimal price.
That is the unregulated monopoly price.
Right: at 6 thousand units the demand price and ATC are both $4.
At $5 buyers want less than 6 thousand units, and the price does not match ATC on demand.

options: Right: the same policy changes MFC differently for a wage taker and a monopsony.

options: That is the socially optimal price, which leaves a loss.
That is the unregulated monopoly's choice.

Right: MC shifts down, so MR = MC at a larger quantity.

options: Right: the firm then produces where MC meets the ceiling.
Right: it lowers MC, raising output.
